## Incident Report — MTA 2026-01-31

**Evidence reviewed:** `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB). No separate IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory. All findings below are derived directly from packet-level analysis with tshark.

**Capture window:** 2026-01-28 03:04:03 → 03:14:27 (local capture timezone +0400), ~10.5 minutes.

---

### 1. Infected / victim host

| Attribute | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** | DHCP, NBNS, all traffic |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** (Intel NIC) | DHCP request, ARP |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | DHCP Option 12, NBNS registration |
| Windows domain/workgroup | WIN11OFFICE (NBNS), member of AD domain **win11office.com** (DC: WIN-LU4L24X3UB7, 10.1.21.2) | NBNS, DNS SRV lookups, SMB2 tree connects |
| Logged-in Windows user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString |

Gateway 10.1.21.1, DNS/DC 10.1.21.2, both on the 10.1.21.0/24 LAN.

### 2. Malware family and attribution

**Behavioral attribution only — not signature-confirmed.** No AV/IDS alert file was provided, and every payload-carrying connection in this capture is TLS-encrypted (the only cleartext HTTP host is the C2 panel itself, which serves a JS check-in script, not a binary). No executable or archive file was observed in cleartext, so no file hash could be extracted from the capture.

Based on the traffic pattern, this matches a **fake-CAPTCHA / "ClickFix"-style malware delivery chain leading to a commodity browser-credential/session stealer**, characterized by:
- A multi-hop domain redirect/TDS (traffic distribution system) chain
- A browser-fingerprinting anti-bot/anti-sandbox gate served in cleartext JavaScript
- Post-infection beaconing to a stealer C2 panel that enumerates and checks in **per browser** (Chrome, then Edge) with an operator ID/token and an explicit `log` action — consistent with a stealer harvesting per-browser data (cookies/credentials/autofill) rather than a generic RAT.

This traffic signature is consistent with the Lumma-Stealer-style "ClickFix" distribution model observed in the wild, but I cannot make a definitive family claim (e.g., "Lumma" vs. a similar stealer-as-a-service kit) without recovering and hashing the actual dropped binary, which was not visible in this capture.

### 3. Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in traffic, all initiated by 10.1.21.58)

**Redirect/delivery chain (DNS + TLS SNI, in chronological order):**

| Time (rel.) | Domain | Resolved IP(s) |
|---|---|---|
| t+45.3s | hiyter.com | 104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145 |
| t+45.8s | media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156, 172.67.154.67 |
| t+48.3s | arch.filemegahab4.sbs | 104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 |

Immediately after the `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` lookup, the host opened a TLS session to **104.21.46.67:443** that transferred **~16 MB inbound** to the victim (largest single conversation in the capture) — consistent with payload delivery, though the content is TLS-encrypted (Cloudflare, using Encrypted Client Hello, so even the true SNI is hidden) and no file name/hash could be recovered.

**Anti-bot fingerprint gate / C2 check-in (cleartext HTTP on TCP/443, confirmed in traffic):**

- **C2 endpoint: 153.92.1.49:443** (domain `whitepepper.su`)
- First contact t+90.3s via `whooptm.cyou` → 62.72.32.156, then t+92.3s to `whitepepper.su`
- Malicious URLs observed:
  - `GET http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
  - `POST http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log`
  - `GET http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?...&agent=Edge`
  - `POST http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?...&agent=Edge&act=log`
- The server response is a browser-fingerprinting JavaScript payload that collects canvas/WebGL/audio/screen/navigator fingerprints, POSTs them back as `URLSearchParams`, then redirects to `about:blank`. The operator ID `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C` and token `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b` identify this specific victim to the panel.
- A follow-on response body states: `cant open archive 172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip` (172.56.88.98 is the victim network's public/NAT egress IP as seen by the C2; the trailing string is a session/fingerprint token embedded in the expected archive filename, not a verified SHA256 of a recovered file).

**Post-gate continuation (further DNS/TLS, likely secondary stager or exfil check):**

| Time (rel.) | Domain | Resolved IP |
|---|---|---|
| t+122.8s | holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 |
| t+126.5s | communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109 |

**Summary IOC list:**
- IPs: `104.21.46.67`, `104.21.48.156`, `104.21.22.231`, `172.67.207.145`, `172.67.154.67`, `172.67.136.13`, `153.92.1.49:443` (C2), `62.72.32.156`, `80.97.160.24`, `104.21.9.36`, `172.67.141.109`
- Domains: `hiyter.com`, `media.megafilehub4.lat`, `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`, `whooptm.cyou`, `whitepepper.su`, `holiday-forever.cc`, `communicationfirewall-security.cc`
- C2 URLs: `whitepepper.su/api/set_agent` (GET/POST, with victim ID `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C` and token `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`)
- No file names or SHA256 hashes could be extracted — all payload-bearing sessions were TLS-encrypted with no observable cleartext transfer of an executable/archive.

**Not flagged:** the SMB2/DCE-RPC traffic to 10.1.21.2 (LSARPC/SAMR over IPC$, GPO `Shared` share access) is standard AD domain-member behavior (logon, Group Policy) and shows no signs of lateral movement or file exfiltration; it is not included as an IOC.
